title: Oceans: The Blue Majority of Earth
summary: The five named oceans, how much of Earth's surface is covered by salt water, and why oceans shape our climate, weather, and trade.
poll: The ocean affects your daily life, even if you live far from the coast.

versions.title: Earth, the Blue Planet
versions.text:
Look at Earth from space. It looks blue. The blue is water. Big seas cover most of our planet. Land is small next to all that water.

We call these big seas oceans. They cover most of Earth's surface. Land covers less. Water covers more.

There are five oceans. Pacific is biggest. Atlantic is next. Indian is warm. Southern is cold. Arctic is icy.

These seas change our weather. The sun warms the sea. Some water goes up into the air. It makes clouds. Clouds make rain. Seas move warm water and cool water, too. This keeps weather mild. Not too hot. Not too cold.

Seas help trade, too. Big ships carry goods. Many things we buy came by ship. A ship costs less than a plane.

Seas are full of life. Fish live there. Whales live there, too. We need the sea to stay well.

versions.title: Oceans: The Blue Majority of Earth
versions.text:
Look closely at a picture of Earth from space. The planet appears mostly blue rather than green or brown. That blue color comes from water, because oceans cover the overwhelming majority of our planet's surface, leaving the continents as a comparatively small patchwork scattered across the globe.

More precisely, oceans cover approximately seventy-one percent of Earth's surface, far more than land does. Land accounts for less than a third of the surface, while salty ocean water covers the remaining, much larger portion. This single fact explains why Earth is sometimes nicknamed the Blue Planet, even though most people instinctively picture it as a world defined by continents and countries.

Geographers divide this enormous body of water into five named oceans, each distinguished by its own size, depth, and climate. The Pacific is by far the largest, containing more water than every continent combined. The Atlantic ranks second in size, separating the Americas from Europe and Africa. The Indian remains warm for most of the year, which strongly shapes the climate of the surrounding lands. The Southern circles the icy continent of Antarctica near the south pole. The Arctic, situated at the top of the world, is the smallest and shallowest of the five.

Oceans regulate Earth's weather and climate every single day. The sun warms the surface of the sea, and some water begins to evaporate, rising into the atmosphere as water vapor. This vapor gathers and cools to form clouds, which eventually release rain over distant land. Oceans also carry warm water and cool water around the globe through immense currents, transporting heat from warm regions toward the much colder ones. This constant circulation keeps the climate in many coastal regions noticeably milder than it would otherwise be.

Oceans also make the vast majority of world trade possible. Enormous cargo ships carry goods across the sea between countries every day, following established shipping routes between major ports. Most of the products people purchase in stores traveled a large share of the distance by ship, because moving goods by sea usually costs far less than moving the same goods by air or over land.

Finally, oceans teem with life of every kind, from microscopic plankton to the largest whales that have ever lived. Fish, sharks, and coral reefs all thrive beneath the waves. People everywhere, even those who live far inland, ultimately depend on healthy oceans in order to live well.

versions.title: Oceans: The Blue Majority of Earth
versions.text:
Anyone who studies a photograph of Earth taken from space will notice something striking: the planet appears overwhelmingly blue rather than green or brown. That blue color comes from water, because oceans cover the vast majority of our planet's surface, leaving the continents as a comparatively small patchwork scattered across the globe.

More precisely, oceans cover approximately seventy-one percent of Earth's surface, far exceeding the area covered by land. Land accounts for less than a third of the surface, while salty ocean water covers the remaining, much larger portion. This single fact explains why Earth is sometimes nicknamed the Blue Planet, even though most people instinctively picture it as a world defined by continents and countries rather than by open water.

Geographers divide this enormous body of water into five named oceans, each distinguished by its own size, depth, and climate. The Pacific is by far the largest, stretching between Asia and the Americas and containing more water than every continent combined. The Atlantic ranks second in size, separating the Americas from Europe and Africa. The Indian remains warm for most of the year, strongly shaping the climate of lands near the equator. The Southern circles the icy continent of Antarctica near the south pole. The Arctic, situated at the top of the world, is the smallest and shallowest of the five.

Oceans regulate Earth's weather and climate through a process oceanographers call ocean circulation. The sun warms surface waters most intensely near the equator, and some of that water begins to evaporate, rising into the atmosphere as vapor and absorbing enormous amounts of heat energy as it does so. This vapor eventually cools, condenses into clouds, and falls as rain over distant land. Meanwhile, massive currents carry warm water and cool water around the globe, transporting heat away from the equator toward the much colder poles. This constant circulation keeps the climate in many coastal regions noticeably milder than it would otherwise be.

Oceans also make the vast majority of world trade possible. Enormous cargo ships carry goods across the sea between countries every day, following established maritime routes between major ports. Most of the products people purchase in stores traveled a large share of the distance by sea, because maritime shipping usually costs far less per ton than moving the same goods by air or over land.

Finally, oceans teem with life of every kind, from microscopic plankton to the largest whales that have ever lived. Fish, sharks, and coral reefs all thrive beneath the waves. People everywhere, even those who live far inland, ultimately depend on healthy oceans in order to live well.

versions.title: Oceans: The Blue Majority of Earth
versions.text:
A photograph of Earth taken from space reveals something immediately striking: the planet appears overwhelmingly blue rather than green or brown, because oceans cover the vast majority of its surface, reducing the continents to a comparatively small patchwork scattered across an otherwise watery globe.

More precisely, oceans cover approximately seventy-one percent of Earth's surface, far exceeding the area occupied by land, which accounts for less than a third of the total. This single fact explains why Earth is occasionally nicknamed the Blue Planet, even though most people instinctively picture it as a world defined primarily by continents and countries rather than by the open water stretching between them.

Geographers divide this enormous body of water into five named oceans, each distinguished by its own size, average depth, and regional climate. The Pacific Ocean is by far the largest, stretching between Asia and the Americas and containing more water than every continent combined, while the Atlantic Ocean ranks second, separating the Americas from Europe and Africa. The Indian Ocean remains warm for most of the year, strongly shaping the climate of lands near the equator, whereas the Southern Ocean circles the icy continent of Antarctica and stays cold regardless of season. The Arctic Ocean, situated at the top of the world, is the smallest and shallowest of the five, and much of its surface remains frozen for a considerable part of the year.

Oceans regulate Earth's weather and climate through a continuous, planet-spanning process oceanographers call ocean circulation. The Sun warms surface waters most intensely near the equator, and some of that water evaporates, rising into the atmosphere as vapor and absorbing enormous quantities of heat energy in the process. This vapor eventually cools, condenses into clouds, and falls as rain over distant land, often thousands of kilometers from the spot where it first evaporated. Meanwhile, massive currents transport warm and cool water around the globe, carrying heat away from the equator toward the far colder poles and keeping coastal climates noticeably milder than they would otherwise be.

Oceans also make the vast majority of world trade possible, since maritime shipping remains, by a wide margin, the cheapest way to move heavy cargo between continents. Enormous container ships follow well-established routes between major ports, and most manufactured goods purchased in stores traveled a large share of their journey by sea rather than by air or by land.

For thousands of years before modern shipping existed, coastal peoples already understood that the sea connected them to distant lands, trading goods, ideas, and even crops along maritime routes that predate written history. The oceans that once separated civilizations gradually became the highways that joined them together.

Finally, oceans teem with life of every imaginable kind, from microscopic plankton to the largest whales that have ever lived, forming food webs on which people everywhere, even those who live far inland, ultimately depend.

LOW.modelAnswer: Oceans matter to everyone because they shape the weather. The Sun warms the sea, and water rises into the air to form clouds that bring rain, even to places far from the coast. Oceans also carry cargo ships that bring goods people buy in stores, so even people who live far inland depend on trade that travels by sea.

keyWords.definition: the usual weather a place has over a long time
keyWords.example: A desert climate is usually hot and dry most of the year.

keyWords.definition: to change from a liquid into a gas, often because of heat
keyWords.example: The puddle began to evaporate once the sun came out.

keyWords.definition: one of the seven huge areas of land on Earth, such as Asia or Africa
keyWords.example: Egypt is a country located on the continent of Africa.

keyWords.definition: goods that are carried by a ship, plane, or truck
keyWords.example: The truck was loaded with cargo for the long trip to the port.

keyWords.definition: to control something so it stays steady or works properly
keyWords.example: A thermostat helps regulate the temperature inside a house.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: The Arctic Ocean is colder than every other ocean on Earth, and no ships cross it.
Oceans cover most of Earth's surface and strongly shape climate and trade.
Coral reefs contain more fish than any other ocean habitat on Earth, so they are most vital.
Cargo ships are the fastest way to move goods between countries, faster than planes.
questions.why: The article's main point is that oceans cover most of Earth's surface and shape both climate and trade.

wrong.A: The Arctic Ocean's coldness is one detail, not the main idea.
wrong.C: Coral reefs are mentioned only briefly near the end.
wrong.D: The article says sea trade is cheaper, not faster, than air trade.

questions.stem: According to the article, about what percentage of Earth's surface is covered by ocean?
options: About 29 percent
About 50 percent
About 71 percent
About 90 percent
questions.why: The article states that oceans cover about seventy-one percent of Earth's surface.

wrong.A: 29 percent is roughly how much of Earth's surface is land, not ocean.
wrong.B: 50 percent is far less than the figure given.
wrong.D: 90 percent is higher than the figure given.

questions.stem: What does the article say shapes the climate of lands around the Indian Ocean?
options: Its cold temperatures all year, even in summer
Its icy surface near the south pole and the ice
Its small, shallow size, with little water in it
Its warm temperatures for most of the year
questions.why: In the article, the Indian Ocean stays warm for most of the year, which shapes the climate of the lands around it.

wrong.A: The Indian Ocean is described as warm, not cold.
wrong.B: An icy surface near the south pole describes the Southern Ocean.
wrong.C: Small, shallow size describes the Arctic Ocean, not the Indian Ocean.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word regulate mean when it says oceans regulate weather and climate?
options: Destroy completely
Control and keep steady
Speed up suddenly
Observe from far away
questions.why: The article explains that oceans keep weather from becoming too hot or too cold, which means they control and steady it.

wrong.A: The article does not say oceans destroy weather.
wrong.C: Oceans are described as keeping weather milder, not speeding it up.
wrong.D: Oceans actively affect weather; they do not just observe it.

questions.stem: What causes clouds to form over the ocean, according to the article?
options: Cold currents freeze the surface of the water.
Warmed sea water evaporates and rises into the air.
Cargo ships stir up water as they pass.
Coral reefs release gas bubbles into the air.
questions.why: In the article, the Sun warms the sea, water evaporates, rises as vapor, and gathers into clouds.

wrong.A: Freezing is not described as causing clouds.
wrong.C: Ships are not linked to cloud formation.
wrong.D: Coral reefs are not linked to cloud formation.

questions.stem: A country has no coastline and is far from any ocean. Based on the article, how would it most likely be affected by changes in the ocean?
options: It would not be affected at all, since it has no coast, and the sea is far from its land.
It could still be affected through changes in rainfall and the cost of imported goods.
It would only be affected if it bordered the Arctic Ocean, and no other ocean could change it.
It would be affected only during the winter season, when the cold ocean winds blow.
questions.why: The article shows that oceans shape rainfall everywhere and that most trade goods travel by sea, so even landlocked countries are affected.

wrong.A: The article argues that even inland places depend on oceans.
wrong.C: The effect described is not limited to countries near the Arctic.
wrong.D: The article does not limit ocean effects to one season.

questions.stem: Why are most goods in stores likely to have traveled by cargo ship rather than by airplane?
options: Airplanes cannot carry heavy cargo of any kind over the ocean.
Moving goods by sea usually costs far less than moving them by air.
Ships can travel faster than airplanes across oceans and seas.
Most countries do not allow airplanes to carry cargo into ports.
questions.why: The article states that trade by sea usually costs much less than trade by air, which explains why ships carry most goods.

wrong.A: The article does not claim airplanes cannot carry cargo.
wrong.C: The article never compares the speed of ships and airplanes.
wrong.D: The article does not mention any rule against air cargo.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the information in this article?
options: By comparing two different planets, such as Mars and Venus, one with the other, over and over
By describing the five oceans and then explaining their effects on climate and trade
By listing oceans from coldest to warmest only, without telling anything about climate or trade
By telling a story about a sea voyage, with a captain, a crew, and many days of travel
questions.why: The article first introduces how much of Earth is ocean, describes each of the five oceans, and then explains their effects on climate and trade.

wrong.A: No other planet is described in detail.
wrong.C: The oceans are not organized strictly by temperature.
wrong.D: There is no voyage story in the article.

MID.prompt: Explain how oceans help regulate Earth's climate. Use details from the article about evaporation and ocean currents.
checklist: I explained how evaporation is part of the process.
I explained how ocean currents move heat around the globe.
I used details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Oceans help regulate Earth's climate because the Sun warms sea water until some of it begins to evaporate, rising into the air and later falling as rain. At the same time, huge ocean currents carry warm water and cool water around the globe, moving heat from warmer areas toward colder ones. Together, evaporation and these currents keep coastal climates milder than they would be without the ocean's influence.

keyWords.definition: the continuous movement of something, such as water or air, around a system
keyWords.example: Ocean circulation moves warm and cool water all around the globe.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the sea, ships, or sailing
keyWords.example: The city grew wealthy because of its busy maritime trade.

keyWords.definition: to take in and hold something, such as heat, light, or liquid
keyWords.example: Dark clothing tends to absorb more heat from the sun than light clothing does.

keyWords.definition: tiny drops of a liquid, such as water, floating in the air as a gas
keyWords.example: Water vapor rising from the warm sea eventually formed clouds.

keyWords.definition: an imaginary line around the middle of Earth, equally far from the north and south poles
keyWords.example: Places near the equator tend to have hot climates all year.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Oceans are almost completely empty of life compared with land ecosystems everywhere.
The Arctic Ocean is more important to world trade than any other ocean.
Oceans cover most of Earth's surface and powerfully shape global climate, trade, and life.
Cargo ships are gradually being replaced by air transport worldwide.
questions.why: The article develops the idea that oceans dominate Earth's surface and have major effects on climate, trade, and living things.

wrong.A: The article describes oceans as teeming with life, not mostly empty.
wrong.B: The Arctic Ocean is described as the smallest and coldest, not the most important for trade.
wrong.D: The article does not claim air transport is replacing ships.

questions.stem: According to the article, which ocean contains more water than every continent combined?
options: The Atlantic Ocean
The Pacific Ocean
The Southern Ocean
The Arctic Ocean
questions.why: The largest ocean holds an enormous amount of water.

wrong.A: The Atlantic Ocean is described only as second in size.
wrong.C: The Southern Ocean circles Antarctica but is not described this way.
wrong.D: The Arctic Ocean is described as the smallest of the five.

questions.stem: Why do massive ocean currents move heat away from the equator toward the poles?
options: Because warm water near the equator is carried by currents toward colder regions.
Because the poles produce their own heat independently, using hot rocks below the ice.
Because cargo ships push warm water toward the poles as they sail across the oceans.
Because the equator has no sunlight at all, so the water there is always very cold.
questions.why: The article explains that currents transport heat from the warm equator toward the colder poles.

wrong.B: The poles are described as colder, not as producing their own heat.
wrong.C: Ships are unrelated to heat transport in the article.
wrong.D: The equator is described as receiving intense sunlight, not none at all.

questions.stem: How does the Sun's warming near the equator compare with its effect at the poles, based on the article?
options: Warming is roughly equal everywhere on Earth.
The Sun warms surface waters most intensely near the equator.
The Sun warms the poles more intensely than the equator.
The Sun's warming effect on oceans is not mentioned.
questions.why: The sea is warmest near the equator.

wrong.A: The article specifically highlights the equator as warmer.
wrong.C: This reverses what the article says.
wrong.D: The Sun's warming effect is a central part of the explanation.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word "circulation" mean?
options: A sudden storm at sea
A single, one-time journey across an ocean
Continuous movement around a system
A method of measuring ocean depth
questions.why: The surrounding sentences describe currents constantly transporting water and heat around the globe, which is continuous movement around a system.

wrong.A: Storms are not described in this part of the article.
wrong.B: The article describes an ongoing, repeating process, not a single trip.
wrong.D: Measuring depth is unrelated to circulation as used here.

questions.stem: If ocean circulation suddenly stopped moving heat from the equator to the poles, what would most likely happen?
options: Coastal climates would probably become more extreme, with hotter tropics and colder poles.
World trade would immediately stop completely, because ships could not sail anywhere on the sea.
The five oceans would merge into a single ocean, and all the islands would sink beneath it.
Rainfall patterns would stay exactly the same everywhere, and nothing would change on Earth at all.
questions.why: Since currents are described as keeping coastal climates milder by moving heat, losing that process would likely make temperature extremes worse.

wrong.B: Trade depends on shipping routes, not directly on heat circulation.
wrong.C: Ocean boundaries are not linked to circulation in the article.
wrong.D: Rainfall depends partly on evaporation driven by this same warming process.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might a landlocked country's economy still be affected by maritime shipping costs?
options: Because most imported goods still travel a large share of their journey by sea before reaching that country.
Because landlocked countries are required to build their own ports on the sea, and this costs money.
Because maritime shipping routes only exist near the equator, and ships never sail anywhere else.
Because cargo ships cannot carry goods meant for landlocked countries, so they use trucks only.
questions.why: The article explains that most goods travel a large share of the distance by sea, so changes in shipping costs would still affect countries without a coastline.

wrong.B: The article never claims landlocked countries must build ports.
wrong.C: Maritime routes connect ports worldwide, not only near the equator.
wrong.D: Goods bound for landlocked countries still typically travel partway by sea.

questions.stem: Why does the author likely include the detail that oceans absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide and heat?
options: To argue that oceans should replace all other forms of trade
To suggest that oceans play a crucial, often unseen role in Earth's climate system
To prove that whales produce most of the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
To explain why the Arctic Ocean is warmer than the equator
questions.why: The detail about absorbing heat and carbon dioxide supports the article's broader point that oceans quietly regulate Earth's climate.

wrong.A: The article discusses trade and climate as separate points, not as replacements for one another.
wrong.C: Whales are not linked to carbon dioxide production in the article.
wrong.D: The article never claims the Arctic Ocean is warmer than the equator.

HIGH.prompt: Some people argue that oceans matter mainly because of trade, while others argue that their role in climate is more important. Take a position and support it with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the ocean's role in climate is more important than its role in trade, even though trade depends on it too. The article explains that ocean circulation moves heat from the warm equator toward the colder poles, keeping coastal climates milder, and that evaporation from the sea's surface is the main source of rain that falls far inland. Without this constant circulation and absorption of heat, weather everywhere, not just near coasts, would likely become far more extreme. Trade could, in theory, shift partly to other methods, but there is no replacement for the climate system that oceans maintain for the entire planet.

LOW.stem: Which ocean does the article call warm?
options: Pacific
Atlantic
Arctic

wrong.A: The Pacific is the biggest ocean, not the warm one.

Clouds make rain at once

Whales swim up to the land

wrong.C: Ships carrying goods is a different topic.

Ships are faster than planes
Ships do not need the sea

wrong.A: The text says big ships carry goods.
wrong.C: The text says a ship costs less, not that it is faster.
wrong.D: Ships sail on the sea.

LOW.stem: The text says oceans cover most of our planet. What does cover mean?

to dig under
to push away
to look at
LOW.why: Oceans spread over most of Earth's surface, so cover means to spread over.

wrong.C: Oceans do not push the land away.

MID.stem: Which ocean is the smallest and coldest of the five?
options: Arctic
Southern
Indian
Atlantic
MID.why: In the article, the Arctic is the smallest and coldest of the five.

wrong.B: The Southern circles the icy continent near the south pole.
wrong.C: The Indian stays warm most of the year.

Fall as heavy rain
Turn to vapor

MID.stem: Why is Earth sometimes nicknamed the Blue Planet?

Its ice is bright blue
Oceans cover most of it

wrong.A: The article says land covers less than a third.
wrong.B: The article says oceans form clouds.
wrong.C: The article does not say the ice is blue.

MID.stem: What can you tell about the sea from the plankton, fish, sharks, coral, and whales in it?

It holds many kinds of life
It has only small animals
It is too cold for coral

wrong.C: Whales are giant animals.

HIGH.stem: How does the article describe the Arctic Ocean?

Smallest and shallowest
Warmest of the five
Second largest in size
HIGH.why: The article says the Arctic is the smallest and shallowest of the five.

wrong.A: The Pacific is the largest.
wrong.C: The Indian remains warm for most of the year.
wrong.D: The Atlantic ranks second in size.

HIGH.stem: The article mentions "maritime shipping." What does maritime mean?
options: By air
Over land
Under ground

HIGH.stem: Why did most products people buy travel a large share of the distance by sea?
options: It costs less per ton
Ships carry fewer goods
Ships follow no routes

wrong.C: The article says ships follow established routes.
wrong.D: Ports are on the coast, not inland.

HIGH.stem: What does the author suggest about how most people picture Earth?
options: As a world of open ice
As a world of busy cities
As a world of only oceans
As a world of continents
HIGH.why: In the article, most people picture a world of continents and countries rather than open water.

wrong.B: The article says continents and countries, not busy cities.
wrong.C: In the article, people picture land more than open water.
